title: Ὄνος ἅλας βαστάζων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 265 (= Perry 180). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A donkey, having salt, was crossing a river.
sentences.i: A donkey with a load of salt was crossing a river.
sentences.n: Salt was carried inland by pack-animal from the coast, so the load is an everyday one; the point is only that it dissolves.

sentences.t: Ὀλισθήσας δέ, ὡς κατέπεσεν εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ, ἐκτακέντος τοῦ ἅλατος, κουφότερος ἐξανέστη.
sentences.tr: Olisthēsas de, hōs katepesen eis to hydōr, ektakentos tou halatos, kouphoteros exanestē.
sentences.l: But having slipped, when he fell down into the water, the salt having melted out, he stood up lighter.
sentences.i: But he slipped, and when he had gone down into the water the salt melted away, and he got up lighter than before.
sentences.n: ἐκτακέντος τοῦ ἅλατος is a genitive absolute — a clause hung on the sentence with no grammatical tie to it, where English says 'now that the salt had melted'. κουφότερος is a predicate comparative describing the state he was in as he rose: he came up lighter than he went down.

sentences.t: Ἡσθεὶς δὲ ἐπὶ τούτῳ, ἐπειδὴ ὕστερόν ποτε σπόγγους ἐμπεφορτισμένος κατά τινα ποταμὸν ἐγένετο, ᾠήθη ὅτι, ἐὰν πάλιν πέσῃ, ἐλαφρότερος διεγερθήσεται, καὶ δὴ ἑκὼν ὤλισθε.
sentences.tr: Hēstheis de epi toutōi, epeidē hysteron pote spongous empephortismenos kata tina potamon egeneto, ōiēthē hoti, ean palin pesēi, elaphroteros diegerthēsetai, kai dē hekōn ōlisthe.
sentences.l: And having been pleased at this, when later on, loaded with sponges, he came to be at a certain river, he thought that, if he should fall again, he would get up lighter; and so he slipped willingly.
sentences.i: Pleased with this, when some time afterwards he found himself at a river loaded with sponges, he supposed that if he fell in again he would come up lighter still; and so he slipped on purpose.
sentences.n: ἐμπεφορτισμένος is a perfect middle participle: he is not being loaded but stands loaded, the cargo already on him. After ᾠήθη ὅτι the Greek keeps the tense of the donkey's own thought — the future διεγερθήσεται — where English shifts it back into 'would get up'. ἑκών, 'willing', does an adverb's work — the fall is his own choice.

sentences.t: Συνέβη δὲ αὐτῷ, τῶν σπόγγων ἀνασπασάντων τὸ ὕδωρ, μὴ δυνάμενον ἐξαναστῆναι ἐνταῦθα ἀποπνιγῆναι.
sentences.tr: Synebē de autōi, tōn spongōn anaspasantōn to hydōr, mē dynamenon exanastēnai entautha apopnigēnai.
sentences.l: But it came about for him, the sponges having drawn up the water, being not able to stand up, to be drowned there.
sentences.i: But the sponges drank up the water, and he could not get to his feet, and there he drowned.
sentences.n: συνέβη with a dative and an infinitive is the corpus's regular way of reporting how a thing turned out. δυνάμενον is accusative, agreeing with the unexpressed subject of the infinitive rather than with the dative αὐτῷ — Greek permits either, and takes the accusative here.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔνιοι διὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπινοίας λανθάνουσιν εἰς συμφορὰς ἐνσειόμενοι.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn enioi dia tas idias epinoias lanthanousin eis symphoras enseiomenoi.
sentences.l: So too, among men, some, through their own contrivances, escape their own notice being flung into misfortunes.
sentences.i: So too, among men, some are flung into disaster by their own clever notions and never see it coming.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle works the reverse of English: ἐνσειόμενοι carries the action and the verb says only that it went unnoticed. ἐπίνοια is the notion that occurs to one — the bright idea, not wisdom.
